saturation_note: Saturation was reached in stages, not all at once. The consumer art-frame segment saturated early (around search 10) - it is genuinely just the known set. The signage/poster segment kept producing new names much longer, through search ~44. The last seven consecutive searches ('e-paper totem', EuroShop exhibitors, 'new company startup 2026', 'product launch Oct-Dec 2026', '42/46 inch consumer frame', 'brand name 2026 minus majors', and the Turkey/Brazil/Poland/UK OEM query) returned only names already recorded, plus an unverifiable tier of anonymous Alibaba OEM/ODM listings. Two important caveats on the saturation claim: (1) Language was the binding constraint, not query count. A single Chinese query found Guangzhou OED - a non-E-Ink panel maker shipping 31.2in colour at 18fps - and a single Japanese query found Teidec's five-size ladder with microSD playback. Neither is reachable in English. Korean was NOT swept and is the most likely remaining gap. (2) Source type mattered more than vocabulary. The epaperia.org member list yielded 13 names in one fetch; the Home Assistant community channel yielded the two most self-hosting-friendly vendors in the entire survey. Both were invisible to product-led searching.

vendors.name: Tisensi
vendors.hardware_track_record: Not a display manufacturer. Builds integrated hardware ecosystems around Sharp panels - customizable design frames from composite materials made of otherwise non-recyclable aluminium and plastic waste, plus a tool-free mounting system. Presented at Digital Signage Summit 2026 with Sharp as technology partner.
vendors.rationale: Three years old, no disclosed funding, and dependent on Sharp for panels. Interesting for the framing/mounting design thinking (which is where most signage products fail as wall art) but too young and too small to build a dependency on.

sources.what_it_supports: Krakow base, founded 2023, sustainability-first stack, composite recycled frames, tool-free mounting, Sharp partnership, CEO Borys Straczek quote about nobody doing e-paper properly. From search results (invidis.com) not directly fetched; URL null per the citation rule.

vendors.name: Etulipa (subsidiary of Miortech)
vendors.ownership: Subsidiary of Miortech (founded 2006 by Hans Feil as a Liquavista spinoff); Etulipa formed 2013
vendors.hardware_track_record: Large-area reflective electrowetting displays for outdoor billboards, using an optical waveguide over tiles to make seams invisible. Full-colour displays consume ~7W per square metre. Partnered with URT (2017) and was in active testing with Daktronics (2022).
vendors.abandonment_history: Long development runway with repeated partner announcements but limited evidence of volume shipping - a yellow flag.
vendors.rationale: The most credible non-electrophoretic reflective technology found, and the tiling approach is genuinely clever. But a decade-plus of partner announcements without clear volume deployment suggests it has not crossed into a real business. Not a route to an art display today.

sources.what_it_supports: Netherlands base, Miortech/Liquavista lineage, 2006 and 2013 founding dates, tiled electrowetting with optical waveguide, ~7W/sqm, URT and Daktronics partnerships. From search results (etulipa.com, e-ink-info.com, sixteen-nine.net) not directly fetched; URL null per the citation rule.

vendors.name: Seeed Studio

vendors.rationale: Well-established in the maker ecosystem with a genuine track record of open documentation. Individual product SKUs come and go, but because the toolchain is open, obsolescence is recoverable. The cheapest credible route to a 13in+ six-colour panel by a wide margin.

sources.what_it_supports: $14.90 board / $163.90 kit pricing, 13.3in Spectra 6 1600x1200, Seeed GFX library on GitHub, Arduino and SenseCraft paths, 2.4GHz-only limitation

sources.what_it_supports: Miami base, UL48/UL879, 13.3in-46in catalogue, 32in with Android 10, 200W solar and 20W/day draw, NYC deployment. From search results (nanov.info, ravepubs.com) not directly fetched; URL null per the citation rule.

leads_not_followed.lead: Korean-language search was never run. Chinese and Japanese searches each produced a major find that no English query surfaced (Guangzhou OED, Teidec).
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: Korea has Samsung, LG and SOLUM all shipping large-format e-paper, so a domestic supplier/integrator tier almost certainly exists and is invisible to English search. This is the single highest-value remaining gap and the main reason my saturation claim should be read as 'saturated in English, Chinese and Japanese' rather than absolutely.

leads_not_followed.lead: epaperia.org's 'Industry Database' and 'ePaper Mall' sections were not enumerated - only the member list on the landing page was. The site claims 260+ member resources; I captured 16.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: This one page produced more new names than any other source in the sweep. The remaining ~244 resources are the densest unexplored vein available, and the ePaper Mall in particular would give product-level data rather than just company names.

leads_not_followed.lead: The Alibaba OEM/ODM tier (Shenzhen Caison, Leeka Electronic, Elsun, Shangtuo Semicon, Startek, Minew, Clientop, Zemso, Veto, Refee, Zhejiang Sunparl, Zhuhai Suny) was recorded as a class but not individually verified. Alibaba reports 762 e-paper-with-WiFi suppliers.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: Mostly reselling Good Display or E Ink panels with generic firmware, so the marginal information value per vendor is low - but this is also where the cheapest 32in colour units live ($549-$1,395 quoted), well below the $1,300-$3,000 branded art frames. Worth one focused pass if price is the binding constraint.

leads_not_followed.lead: Samsung's 32in EMDX retail SKU advertises USB Type-C compatibility, and Nanov's 32in runs Android 10.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: These are the two most promising undocumented local-push surfaces found. A USB-C port that accepts an image, or an Android controller reachable over ADB, would each bypass the cloud CMS entirely on hardware that is otherwise closed. Neither is documented anywhere I looked; both are testable with a unit in hand.

leads_not_followed.lead: Cayin Technology's claim to connect with 'any e-paper device, regardless of brand, model or size' was not technically verified.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: If real, it is a brand-agnostic content layer across otherwise incompatible panels - which would change the buying calculus from 'pick the vendor with the best API' to 'pick the best panel'. The press coverage contained no protocols, no API detail, and no supported-device list, so it may be marketing.

leads_not_followed.lead: paperlesspaper's API docs were only read at the landing-page level. Whether the API terminates locally on the device or requires paperlesspaper's servers was not resolved.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: This is the decisive question for the single best self-hosting candidate found. Open hardware plus a cloud-dependent API would be materially less useful than it appears. The endpoint reference and Getting Started sections would settle it.

leads_not_followed.lead: Guangzhou OED's own website, pricing, and panel availability to third parties were not investigated.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: OED is the only credible second source of large colour reflective panels. Whether it sells bare panels or driver boards to outsiders determines whether it can break E Ink's pricing power for DIY builders, or only for its OEM partners.

leads_not_followed.lead: Teidec's distribution outside Japan, pricing, and resolutions were not established.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: Teidec's microSD standalone mode on a 40.5in A1 colour panel is the only fully offline path to a large colour display found in the entire sweep. If it can be bought outside Japan at a sane price, it is arguably the best answer to the brief's underlying question.

leads_not_followed.lead: Sharp's ePoster A0 (57in) and A1 (40in) models were referenced only via a secondary description of the size ladder, not confirmed on Sharp's own product pages.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: 57in would be the largest non-tiled reflective panel in the survey. The size ladder came from an invidis summary of Sharp's range rather than a Sharp source, so it needs confirmation.

leads_not_followed.lead: Trade-show exhibitor lists were sampled (Touch Taiwan, ISE, InfoComm, EuroShop) but never enumerated systematically - I read coverage of the shows rather than the raw exhibitor directories.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: The one exhibitor list I did touch produced Hanjentek and M2COMM, neither of which any product search found. Walking the actual ISE and InfoComm e-paper exhibitor directories would likely produce a similar yield of integrator-tier names.

leads_not_followed.lead: LINKUADRO could not be verified - the Kickstarter page returned HTTP 403 and no secondary coverage carried specifications.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: It is the only genuinely unrecorded consumer art-frame brand found, but sizes, price and whether it exceeds 13in are all unknown, so it cannot be placed in or out of scope.

leads_not_followed.lead: Ynvisible (electrochromic, used by Waypoint Transit Solutions) and Plastic Logic (flexible), CLEARink, and Azumo were identified as non-E-Ink reflective players but not sized or specced.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: These are segment-adjacent rather than art-relevant - Ynvisible's displays are segmented/low-information rather than pixel-addressable - but they represent the alternative-technology branch that could eventually produce a cheaper large reflective panel.

unverified_facts.claim: paperlesspaper's openpaper L can be driven entirely from a local server with no dependency on paperlesspaper's cloud.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The product page and the API docs landing page both confirm an open-source device and a documented API, but neither states where the API terminates. I did not read the endpoint reference. Plausible given the open-hardware stance, but not established.

unverified_facts.claim: Glory Star's 'Star Control' is a local/LAN image-push tool rather than a cloud service.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The e-paper landing page names Star Control and links a tutorial, but does not say whether it is desktop software, a LAN service or a cloud platform. The detailed product page was truncated on fetch.

unverified_facts.claim: Nanov's 32in Android 10 controller exposes ADB, allowing direct image push.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Android 10 is confirmed as the built-in system by product coverage, but ADB availability is my inference from the platform, not a documented vendor capability. Commercial signage builds frequently disable ADB.

unverified_facts.claim: Cayin's e-paper integration genuinely works with any e-paper device regardless of brand.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: This is the vendor's own claim as reported in trade press. No protocols, no API surface and no supported-device list were published, and I found no independent verification.

unverified_facts.claim: Sharp's ePoster line spans A3 20in, A2 28in, A1 40in and A0 57in.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: This size ladder came from an invidis article describing Sharp's range in the context of the Tisensi partnership, not from Sharp's own product documentation. The separately confirmed Sharp products are the 42in monochrome, 25.3in and 13.3in.

unverified_facts.claim: Guangzhou OED's 31.2in panel is available for purchase by third parties.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Coverage says OED 'is making and shipping' 31.2in colour displays, but does not say to whom or in what form (bare panel, module, or only through the Geniatech partnership). I did not fetch OED's own site.

unverified_facts.claim: Samsung's 32in EMDX USB Type-C port accepts image content for display.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The Amazon retail listing advertises 'USB Type-C Compatibility' but does not say what that means functionally - it may be power-only, or for firmware/service. No documentation found either way.

unverified_facts.claim: Teidec's e-paper signage is purchasable outside Japan.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The product page is Japanese-language with no international ordering path, no pricing and no distributor list. Japan-only distribution is likely but not confirmed.

unverified_facts.claim: Visionect has substantially exited hardware in favour of software.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Based on an invidis headline and summary from February 2026 ('E-Paper Pioneer Shifts Focus to Software'). I did not fetch the article body, so the extent of the shift - and whether Place & Play hardware remains orderable - is unestablished. This matters because Visionect has been the default self-hostable 32in option.

unverified_facts.claim: The 'E Ink D-Poster' (32in Spectra 6, 3060x2160, 130 PPI, ~17s per image transition, Bluetooth 5.2, 4kg) is a purchasable product rather than a reference design.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: These specifications came from a Good e-Reader summary returned in search results. The custom CMS mentioned suggests a reference/OEM design rather than a retail SKU, and it does not appear in the E Ink shopkit catalogue I fetched.

unverified_facts.claim: The various 31.5in posters sold by StellarLink, AUO Display Plus, TCL CSOT, Hanjentek, Glory Star, Praevar and SwitchBot are substantially the same underlying AUO/E Ink hardware.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The StellarLink aecoPost is explicitly confirmed as AUO Display Plus manufactured, and AUO has a confirmed large-format JV with E Ink. Extending that to the other 31.5in products is a reasonable inference from the convergent 2560x1440 Spectra 6 spec, but it is an inference, not a documented fact.

unverified_facts.claim: Melford Technologies manufactures rather than resells its e-paper displays.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The company self-describes as a manufacturer with 50+ years in display technology, and the fetched page presents the range as its own. But the size ladder (13.3/25.3/28/32/42/75in) maps exactly onto E Ink's standard catalogue, which is more consistent with integration than panel manufacture.
